title: Talk Is Cheap
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky synthesizes a 2025 paper by Corbin, Dawson & Liu introducing the discursive/structural distinction in AI governance for education assessment. Discursive changes (traffic light systems, scaffolded AI workflows, declaration forms) attempt to elicit compliance through language alone without enforcement mechanisms. Structural changes alter the nature of the assessment task itself, creating environments where desired behavior emerges naturally from design rather than from voluntary compliance. The enforcement illusion: AI traffic lights borrow the visual logic of real traffic enforcement infrastructure while possessing none of its actual enforcement capacity -- real traffic lights work because they are embedded in cameras, penalties, and physical infrastructure, not because they are visible. Studies show up to 74% of students at one major institution did not complete AI declaration requirements appropriately. The discursive/structural distinction clarifies what category most school AI governance belongs to and what category it cannot reach. True structural responses include oral examinations, authenticated checkpoints, and evidentiary chains built across a unit. Potkalitsky's own 5-orientation AI literacy framework (Critic, Verifier, Interlocutor, Editor, Architect) sits at the boundary -- discursive when communicated as orientations, potentially structural when embedded in how tasks are sequenced across a year.
points: * Discursive changes operate through linguistic commands and attempt to elicit compliance without enforcement mechanisms; structural changes alter the mechanics of the task itself so desired behavior emerges naturally from the design. * The enforcement illusion: real traffic lights work because of cameras, penalties, and physical infrastructure; AI traffic lights for academic integrity have the visual logic of enforcement without any of its actual capacity. * Studies show up to 74% of students at one major institution did not complete AI declaration requirements appropriately -- policy existed, compliance did not. * Communication, however clear, detailed, or earnest, cannot do what only structure can do -- most of what schools have built in response to generative AI is discursive, and that work has value, but it does not protect assessment validity. * True structural responses include oral examinations, authenticated checkpoints, and evidentiary chains built across a unit -- but these are artisanal, expensive, and reintroduce the labor costs that scalable online assessment was designed to eliminate.
quotes: Many schools now have an AI policy... And yet, for the most part, none of it is working in the way we hoped for and imagined.
Discursive changes operate through what might be called linguistic commands -- they attempt to elicit compliance through language alone, without corresponding mechanisms to enforce those boundaries.
Structural changes alter the nature, format, or mechanics of the task itself -- create assessment environments where the desired behaviour emerges naturally from the assessment design.
We are using the language of structural change to describe what are purely discursive interventions.
When assessment validity rests on student compliance with unenforceable rules, we are not protecting the integrity of our credentials so much as assuming it, quietly, at scale.
communication, however clear, however detailed, however earnest, cannot do what only structure can do.
Most of what schools have built in response to generative AI is discursive. That work has value, but it does not protect assessment validity.
